source.title: Random Features Model with General Convex Regularization: A Fine Grained Analysis with Precise Asymptotic Learning Curves
source.authors: David Bosch; Ashkan Panahi; Ayça Özçelikkale; Devdatt P. Dubhashi

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies random-feature model width and measures generalization error around the interpolation threshold, testing double-descent behavior with a synthetic, regularized random-features setup rather than the original deep-network settings.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites double-descent findings from prior work; those cited results are not rows. Figure 2 varies lambda at fixed model-to-data ratios and reports an optimal lambda for each ratio, but does not test whether an optimally tuned regularizer removes the size-wise peak.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps random-features width ratio γ=m/n under elastic-net regularization (Fig. 1b). It reports a generalization-error spike at the interpolation threshold that shrinks as regularization grows. This bears on V4 (a non-deep model class) and V6 (regularization dependence). Double descent is a side result of a theory paper, in a new setting, so T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The main conclusion is theoretical: exact asymptotic learning curves for square-loss RF models with strongly convex or ℓ1 regularization, via a 4-D scalar optimization, plus universality extended to elastic net and ℓ1. Experiments show the predictions match simulations, with discrepancy only near the interpolation peak. The observation that regularization diminishes the peak is a secondary remark, presented as consistent with prior double-descent work.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and simulates synthetic, square-loss random-features regression with elastic-net regularization, varying m/n; this differs from the original deep-network size-sweep settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The height of the interpolation peak depends on regularization strength α; the paper reports that it diminishes as α increases.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
record.problems: The empirical study uses synthetic data and a random-features model, with n + m = 1000 and 100 random realizations per empirical point. The generalization-error curves are provided in figures without numerical values or reported uncertainty bars; the study does not test epochs or sample-count sweeps.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 varies λ at fixed γ and reports a λ minimizing expected error for each ratio. It does not compare model-size curves under optimally tuned regularization, so it does not directly measure the peak behavior in V6.

untested.parts: Only a random-features model (one-hidden-layer network with fixed random weights); no deep networks.
No sweep over epochs or training time.
There is no sample-count sweep at fixed model size; n and m co-vary with n+m=1000, so a 'more data hurts' effect cannot be isolated.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak location.
Label noise is not varied (σε²=0.1 fixed). There is no test of triple or multiple descent. There is no test that optimally tuned regularization removes the peak across γ.
No re-expression in an effective number of parameters.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 limits_scope label is dropped: the absence of an optimal-regularization test is an untested part, not a limitation. With n+m fixed, the γ sweep changes sample count and width together, so it is not a clean model-size sweep. Figure 2 (optimal λ per γ) is declared in rows_left_out; its curves cannot be read numerically from the text. There are no uncertainty bars, and values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: The model-size experiment is on a random-features model described as a neural network with one hidden layer, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The experiment varies model width relative to sample count, not the number of training samples near a fixed interpolation threshold.
The model-size/generalization-error curve is tested only for the paper's random-features model and synthetic data, not across a range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, or sample count.

The experiment varies regularization strength and reports its effect on the interpolation peak. It does not vary label noise, test triple or multiple descent, or show that an optimally tuned regularizer eliminates the peak.
The curve is not re-expressed using an effective number of parameters.
